notes.body:
The ruling that prayer behind a bedouin (أَعْرَابِيّ) imam is void rests on a legal principle: **the imam's religious fitness is a precondition for the congregation's prayer to be valid**. When we pray behind an imam, our prayer attaches to his — spiritually and legally. If his standing before Allah is compromised, that bond breaks.

The Quranic characterization is the legal evidence. Allah says:

الْأَعْرَابُ أَشَدُّ كُفْرًا وَنِفَاقًا وَأَجْدَرُ أَلَّا يَعْلَمُوا حُدُودَ مَا أَنزَلَ اللَّهُ عَلَىٰ رَسُولِهِ
The bedouins are harder in disbelief and hypocrisy and more likely to be unaware of the limits of what Allah has revealed to His Messenger.
At-Tawbah 9:97

Notice that final phrase: *unaware of the limits of what Allah revealed*. An imam **must know those limits to lead others across them correctly**; when Allah Himself declares a group likely to lack that knowledge — and deeper in disbelief (كفر) and hypocrisy (نفاق) than most — the law treats that declaration as disqualifying them from leading prayer.

The man in the passage had also emigrated, crossing into a higher religious covenant. **Praying behind someone the Quran places at the outermost edge of the believing community** directly contradicts the act of migration he had undertaken — which is why his emigrant status intensifies rather than excuses the ruling.

A surgeon's assistant cannot hand the scalpel to someone unlicensed to hold it, even if the operation itself proceeds correctly. **The content of the man's prayer was sound; what failed was the authority through which it was communally offered.**

etymology: نفاق (hypocrisy): from the root ن-ف-ق, whose core noun is نَفَق — a tunnel or burrow with two openings, one visible entry and one hidden exit. The hypocrite enters from one side while planning escape from the other. The image captures the double life the word names: a person whose outward faith conceals an entirely different interior.

كفر (disbelief): from the root ك-ف-ر, meaning to cover or conceal. Pre-Islamic Arabic used كافر for a farmer who buries seeds beneath the soil, covering them over. Applied to faith, كفر is the act of burying — beneath habit, pride, or indifference — a truth that has already been placed clearly before you.

أَعْرَابِيّ (bedouin): from the root ع-ر-ب, whose verbal form عَرَّبَ means to make something clear or articulate. Yet أَعْرَابِيّ names one defined by distance from settled communal life — the very life in which religious clarity is forged. The root illuminates the irony: those who carry the language in its purest desert form stand furthest from its spiritual cultivation.

notes.body:
Making up missed prayers follows a strict ranked sequence:

- the obligatory prayers (فرائض) first,
- then the even prayer (شفع) and the odd prayer (وتر),
- then the recommended prayers (سنن).

Two rakahs performed as a matched pair, the even prayer (شفع) is **the night prayer's paired prelude** — it comes immediately before the odd prayer (وتر) at the close of the night prayer sequence, like two hands cupped together before the final release. Together they form the concluding portion of the night prayer that Maulana Ali described as a benefit to the body, an opening to mercy, and a holding fast to the character of the prophets.

The odd prayer (وتر) earns its middle rank because its very name carries the fragrance of divine oneness — a single concluding act that **seals night worship with an echo of Allah's singularity**. In the tradition described here, it consists of three units with the qunut supplication. Because it points so directly toward divine uniqueness, several jurists consider it close to binding, which is why it outranks ordinary recommended prayers.

The recommended prayers (سنن) are the prayers that frame each obligatory prayer — rakahs before and after the prescribed times, following the Prophet's habitual practice. They enrich worship and deepen its quality, but they carry **no urgency of obligation**; they are the gentle, well-worn groove of a prophetic life.

This hierarchy carries real practical weight: when a person dies and leaves a bequeathed sum for making up their missed prayers, the sequence is applied in order:

1. Obligatory prayers (فرائض) first.
2. Then the even prayer (شفع) and the odd prayer (وتر).
3. Then the recommended prayers (سنن), to whatever the remaining wage allows.

notes.quote: then the shaf and the witr, then the sunan
etymology: شفع (the even prayer): from the root ش-ف-ع, meaning to be even-numbered, to pair, or to come in twos. The derived word names the two rakahs that stand together before the witr. Beautifully, the same root gives شفاعة (intercession) — where one soul pairs itself with another to plead before Allah, two voices becoming one appeal.

وتر (the odd prayer): from the root و-ت-ر, meaning to be singular, solitary, or odd-numbered. The name mirrors the prayer's purpose: a single act standing alone at the close of night worship. The root also evokes a taut bowstring — stretched, solitary, releasing with finality — which captures exactly what the witr does to the night prayer.

سنة (recommended practice): from the root س-ن-ن, meaning to establish a smooth, well-worn path or to set a flowing precedent. The سنة is the Prophet's habitual groove — a path so often traveled it becomes natural. The root suggests something fluid and precedent-setting, not sharp or commanded, which is precisely why سنن prayers rank lowest in the hierarchy.

فريضة (obligatory prayer): from the root ف-ر-ض, meaning to cut, to notch, or to prescribe with precision. What is فرض has been notched into the law — fixed and non-negotiable, like a groove carved into wood. The same root yields فرضة, a fixed landing-place on a riverbank: something precisely located and impossible to move.

notes.body:
Specific procedures are left unnamed here, with a deliberate pointer toward 'the books of the friends of God' — the Imams and the senior figures of the Ismaili Da'wa — as the proper source of instruction. This is characteristic of how Ismaili religious writing handles sensitive detail: it lives in authorized transmission through the Da'wa hierarchy, not in texts laid open to every reader.

The word 'release' (إطلاق) carries the image of untying a knot; in religious usage, it means freeing a soul from the binding weight of unmet obligations and accumulated sins. The release involves **specific supplications and intercessions** made on her behalf by the living, asking Allah to untie what had bound her.

'Discharge' (إبراء) is a legal term meaning to formally clear someone of an outstanding claim. Spiritually, this means making good the religious debts she left behind:

- making up her missed prayers (قضاء الصلوات) by proxy
- completing her missed fasts, or paying their ransom (فدية)
- settling any expiations (كفارات) still owed

Among all the deeds one can send on her behalf, **the pilgrimage** (الحج) stands above everything else — Imam Jafar al-Sadiq's reply to his companion makes this unmistakably clear: even giving a mountain's weight in charity would not reach the reward of a single Hajj. If her faith and prayer were uncertain, making up her prayers becomes the most urgent task, because prayer (الصلاة) is, as Maulana Ali taught, the pillar of the religion and the first thing Allah examines of a person's deeds. Ongoing charity (صدقة جارية) flowing to the believers is also among the doors of goodness one can open on her behalf.

notes.quote: her release and her discharge, which are known in the books of the friends of God
etymology: إطلاق (release): from the root ط-ل-ق, carrying the sense of flowing free, being unbound. The verb طَلَّقَ means to release or divorce — to sever a binding tie. إطلاق is the noun of that act: the untying itself. When applied to a soul weighed down by unmet debts, it names the moment the knot is cut and the burden falls away.

إبراء (discharge): from the root ب-ر-أ, meaning to be clear, innocent, free of defect or claim. The root gives بَرِيء (innocent) and بُرْء (recovery from illness — being cleared of it). إبراء is the act of formally clearing someone of an obligation, as a creditor releases a debtor. Spiritually, it is acquittal turned into action.

قضاء (making up): from the root ق-ض-ي, meaning to decide, complete, settle finally. The root gives قَاضٍ (judge) and قَضِيَّة (case, affair). قضاء in prayer law means performing what was owed after its time passed — a verdict of completion, carrying the finality of a judge's ruling.

كفارة (expiation): from the root ك-ف-ر, meaning to cover or conceal. The same root gives كَافِر — one who covers over truth. كفارة is a compensating deed placed over a sin in the scales, covering it. It does not erase; it buries.

notes.body:
The principle al-Muizz draws on is elegant: in Islamic legal reasoning, **a prayer's classification as a night prayer and the fasting person's right to eat share the same boundary line.** The fast (الصوم) of Ramadan is governed by one rule — night is the period when eating is permitted, and day is when it is forbidden. If a prayer belongs to "the night," its time is when the faster may eat.

That logic is a precise test:

1. If Fajr were a night prayer, its time would fall within the night.
2. Night time is, legally, the period when eating is permitted for the fasting person.
3. But at Fajr, eating stops — the fast begins.
4. Therefore Fajr cannot belong to the night.

Night and day here are not just astronomical facts; they are **legal territories** with distinct rulings that switch over at precise thresholds.

This is exactly why al-Muizz places Fajr in a class of its own — "one set midway between all four, belonging to neither the night's division nor the day's division." It is the prayer of the threshold. The Prophet's own words confirm its singular standing:

صَلَاةُ الْغَدَاةِ يَحْضُرُهَا مَلَائِكَةُ اللَّيْلِ وَمَلَائِكَةُ النَّهَارِ
"The morning prayer is attended by the angels of the night and the angels of the day."

No other prayer shares that witness. The passage also describes Fajr as a دَعْوَة (a call or summons) that has no call after it — the final summons before the full weight of the day descends.

notes.quote: if it belonged to the night prayer, the fasting person would be permitted to eat at its time
etymology: دَعْوَة: from root د-ع-و, meaning to call out or summon. Related words: دَعَا (he called), دُعَاء (supplication — the act of calling out to Allah), دَاعِي (the caller). A دَعْوَة is a single act of summoning. Here each prayer is a divine call; Fajr is the last — a call after a preceding call, yet with no call following it.

بَعْدَ: from root ب-ع-د, whose core meaning is distance or remoteness. Related words: بَعِيد (far away), بُعْد (distance itself). When Arabic says بَعْدَ (after), it casts time as space — what comes 'after' lies at a remove from what came before. In the passage, Fajr is a call بَعْدَ a prior call, yet with nothing بَعْدَهَا — after it.
